title: What is a webcast? A plain-English guide
summary: What is a webcast? Learn how webcasting works, how it differs from a webinar, and how to host one with Zoom Webinars & Events.
body_markdown:
A webcast is a direct way to put your message in front of a large audience without booking a venue. If you've watched a company keynote, a product launch, or a town hall from your laptop, you've already seen one in action. So what is a webcast, exactly, and how does it differ from the webinars your team may already run? This guide walks through the definition, how webcasting works, the main types, and how to host your own. If you already present online, many of the habits behind[hosting engaging and memorable webinars](https://www.zoom.com/en/blog/host-engaging-webinars/) carry straight over.

## What is a webcast?


**A webcast is a live or recorded audio and video presentation streamed over the internet from one source to many viewers at once.**[Merriam-Webster](https://www.merriam-webster.com/dictionary/webcast) defines it as "a transmission of sound and images (as of an event) via the Internet." Think of it as a broadcast, delivered over the web.


Webcasting is the process of producing and streaming that content. The presenter, or a small group of presenters, does most of the talking, and the audience mostly watches and listens.


Most webcasts share a few traits:


- **One-to-many delivery.** A single source reaches a large, often distributed audience.
- **Mostly one-way communication.** Viewers may send questions, but the focus is the presentation.
- **Flexible timing.** A webcast can stream live, be watched later on demand, or both.
- **Easy access.** Viewers usually join through a link in a web browser or an app, with no special equipment beyond a device and an internet connection.


## How does a webcast work?


A webcast works by capturing audio and video, converting it into a format that can travel over the internet, and delivering it to viewers through a streaming platform. Here's the basic flow:


1. **Capture.** Cameras, microphones, and screen sharing record the presenter, slides, or demo.
2. **Encode.** Encoding is the process of compressing raw audio and video into a digital stream that can be sent online. Many webcasting platforms handle this step for you.
3. **Stream.** The platform sends the encoded stream to viewers, typically through a registration page or a direct link.
4. **Watch.** Viewers open the link and watch in a browser or app on their computer or phone.
5. **Replay.** The session is recorded so people who missed it, or want a second look, can watch it on demand.


For a simple webcast, a laptop with a good webcam and a headset can cover the capture step. Larger productions might add multiple cameras, a dedicated producer, and branded graphics.


## Webcast vs. webinar: what's the difference?


The main difference between a webcast and a webinar is interaction. A webcast is built mainly for one-way delivery to a large audience, while a webinar is built for presenters to engage attendees in real time through tools like Q&A, polls, and chat. A podcast, by comparison, is usually audio-first and listened to on demand.


Webcast Webinar Podcast


Primary goal Broadcast a message to a wide audience Teach, demo, or discuss with an engaged audience Share episodic audio content


Audience interaction Limited, often Q&A only Built in: chat, Q&A, polls, reactions Usually none during playback

In practice, the line blurs. Many webinar platforms can run a broadcast-style webcast or a highly interactive session, depending on how you set it up. If you want your audience to participate, our guide on[how to run a webinar](https://www.zoom.com/en/blog/how-to-run-a-webinar-your-during-event-strategy-guide/) covers ways to keep people engaged during the session.


## Types of webcasts


### Live webcasts


A live webcast streams in real time. It's the right choice when timing matters, such as a product announcement, a company update, or a keynote people want to watch together. Live webcasts create urgency, and they let you take a few audience questions as they come in.


### On-demand webcasts


An on-demand webcast is a recording viewers can watch whenever it suits them. It extends the life of a live event and works well for training content, evergreen presentations, and audiences across many time zones.


### Pre-recorded webcasts run as live


You can also pre-record a session and run it as live at a scheduled time. Viewers get the shared experience of a live event, while presenters get the confidence of a polished, edited recording. Some teams pair the recording with a live Q&A at the end.


## Common ways to use a webcast


Webcasts can fit many situations where you need to reach a lot of people with the same message. Common uses include:


- **Company all-hands and town halls** that keep remote and in-office employees on the same page
- **Product launches and announcements** that reach customers, partners, and press at the same moment
- **Training and education** that can be streamed live and reused on demand
- **Marketing events and thought leadership** that build awareness with a broad audience
- **Conferences and keynotes** that extend an in-person event to people who can't attend

## Frequently asked questions about webcasts


### What's the difference between a webinar and a webcast?


A webcast is mainly a one-way broadcast to a large audience, while a webinar is designed for real-time interaction between presenters and attendees. Webinars typically include tools like Q&A, polls, and chat. Webcasts may offer limited interaction, such as submitted questions, but the focus stays on the presentation.


### What does webcasting mean?


Webcasting means streaming audio and video content over the internet from one source to many viewers. If you're asking what is a webcast in the simplest terms, it's a broadcast delivered online. Webcasting can happen live or be recorded for on-demand viewing.


### How do I view a webcast?


To view a webcast, open the link the host shares, usually in a registration confirmation or invitation email. Most webcasts play in a web browser or an app on your computer or phone. You'll need a stable internet connection and, for live events, to join at the scheduled time.


### Is a webcast a video?


A webcast is usually a video, but not always.[Collins English Dictionary](https://www.collinsdictionary.com/dictionary/english/webcast) describes a webcast as an event you can listen to or watch on the internet, so some webcasts are audio only. Most business webcasts combine video, audio, and shared slides or screens.

A webcast lets you share one message with a large audience, live or on demand. Once you know whether you need a one-way broadcast or a two-way conversation, choosing the right format gets easier. Zoom Webinars & Events gives you room to do both from the same platform.
